In my election, the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) and the hon. the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Muloek) came in and took a hand. They paid a great deal of attention to the down-trodden farmer, and I was very much pleased to listen to the Minister of Customs, as with his persuasive tone and his patriarchial appearance, he declaimed to the unsophisticated farmer, who could hardly help believing him as he said : Gentlemen, when we came into power what did we find? We found the great Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, which presides over your interests, controlled by a professional man, a doctor. And what did we do ? We brought in a practical farmer, like yourselves, a man who is used to toil with his hands ; he knows how to sympathize with you. I was a little curious when I came down here to see the Minister

of Agriculture. As the ministers came in at the door, I asked wliicli was the Minister of Agriculture. And when he was pointed out to me, I smiled. I would suggest a reorganization of that cabinet, and I would give the portfolio of Agriculture to such a man as my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson). If that were done, you could go to the country and say to the farmers : We have for Minister of Agriculture a practical farmer, a man like yourselves. It was stated, I think by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie.) that when this government came into power in 1896, they introduced a new tariff, and that tariff was criticised-it was fought tooth and nail, as he said-by the Conservatives, who said that if it was brought into force it would ruin this country. They did oppose that tariff, and they did say that it would ruin this country. And, after the government had listened to the criticism, they withdrew that tariff in order to revise it. And they sought the help in revising it of a very estimable gentleman, a clearheaded man. the late lamented member for Centre Toronto. Mr. Geo. Bertram, a man I knew well and respected highly, a former resident of the town in which I now live. He changed that tariff for them and saved the government. Was it not a peculiar thing that the government should call in one of these * scoundrels great and scoundrels small ' to assist them in revising their tariff ? We know that when the Conservatives were on that side of the House, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) used to say that if his party got into power the tariff would be revised in the interests of the farmer. The farmers of Manitoba were told that agricultural implements would be put on the free list. But the tariff on agricultural implements remained just what it was before. But, the government said : We will have to do something for the farmers, for there are a great many of them, and some of them may vote against us. We must give them a sop of some kind. And so they put Indian corn on the free list. It has been a question among farmers themselves whether that was a good thing or not. If a farmer is a Reformer he is apt to say that it was a good thing, and if he is a Conservative he may argue the other way. But there is one thing I noticed -that the pork buyers have been advising their buyers to keep clear of the districts where this Indian corn is ted to make pork, because it destroys the pork for the British market. When this business government knew that the farmers had been seeking for years a market for their barley in the United States, why did they not, instead of taking the duty off corn at once, say to the United States : We will give you a market for your corn if you will give us a market for our barley. But that was not done. The interest of the farmers was lost sight o1'. i Mr. VROOMAN
Our farmers, particularly those of Ontario, have been for years and years looking for a market in the United States for their barley. That market was a great thing for them before the duty of 30 cents a bushel was imposed by the Americans. The government put another thing on the free list -binder twine ; and we hear on the floor of the House that some of the supporters of the government are not satisfied. One thing we know, and that is that when binder twine was put on the free list, the price of it went up. And when barbed wire was put on the free list, the price of it went up also. Some other things were put on the free list-mushroom spawn, for instance.
And ice.

Was ice put on the free list ? I am glad to hear that. But I would like to ask how the farmer was helped by putting the duty on sugar ? There is a question which touches every man. A little additional duty was put on cottons also, and on tobacco. The labouring man likes to take a smoke at the end of his hard day's work. But when he sends out his little boy with a five-eent piece for a plug of tobacco, the boy comes back and says : I want another cent. It is true that to meet that, the manufacturers have cut the size of the plug down to fit the charge so as to leave it five cents. We have delegations coming to this government, and it is right that they should come. But when a delegation comes in the interest of the farmers, how are they received ? Farmers are not millionaires, but men of moderate means. There was a delegation came here the other day in the interests of the beetroot sugar industry, and this government gave them the go-by. But, I would refer the Minister of Agriculture to what the Minister of Agriculture in Ontario has done. Of course, I understand very well that the Ontario minister expects an election soon. Still, it is a wonderful statement he makes. He says that Ontario can grow 109.000,000 pounds of sugar annually. I think he knows what he is talking about, because he has been an efficient minister there for many years. This would employ a million and a half of people. It has been proven that the farmers can clear a profit of $43.50 per acre in raising beet root. And the Ontario government have agreed to give to that industry $75,000 annually for three years. But when the farmers came down here they got no help. Yet. the government could make concessions to a lot of Standard Oil magnates when they came here-millionaires from the United States. It was stated here the other night that when this government came in they reduced the duty on coal oil from 7 cents to 5 cents a gallon. Of course, that was a mistake-what was meant was that they reduced it from 6 cents to o cents a gallon. But concessions
have been made to the Standard Oil Company, and the result is that oil was never so dear in Ontario as it has been since. The condition of things is this-if you go into a store with your can and ask the dealer for a gallon of American oil, he will give you what he calls American oil, but you never know whether it is American oil or not. I understand that the oil inspection of this country is practically no inspection at all. The Standard Oil Company has a monopoly of the oil business in this country. I would ask the government why they have not reduced the duty on coal oil so as to make oil cheaper. There was a time when it was necessary to protect the oil industry in the interest of the country. But now that it is in the hands of foreigners, why should we protect it ?
Now, as to this preference, I have looked at it, read about it, and considered it; and, so far as the farmer is concerned, I cannot see that it is of any use to him at all. If it is true that many of his products were imported into England last year, but that would have been so in any case. There was an increase, because there was an increase in all branches of that kind of business. But the preference had nothing to do with it. If the farmers receive no benefit from the preference as it is to-day, they are on the other hand directly injured in the German market.
Now, when this government undertook to give a preference to England in our markets why did they not ask the English government to remove the embargo on our cattle? Before this embargo was placed on our cattle they had a preference in the English market, as there was at that time an embargo on American cattle. Every head of cattle taken into England from Canada was worth $10 or $15 more than a like animal from the United States. That embargo was put on our cattle ostensibly because there was pleuro-pneumonia among them, when in reality there was not. Before the embargo our cattle, after landing in England, were taken into the country and fed for two or three weeks on the rich grasses of England, until the beef attained a flavour like that of English beef, and became more toothsome to the fastidious palate of John Bull. Now, when our government gave a preference to English goods, they should have said to the English gov-erment: We have given you this preference in our market, now we want you to take the embargo off our cattle. But the Prime Minister says we did not want to ask anything in return from the English government, that what we were giving them was out of pure gratitude for the many favours we had received from them in the past and were still receiving.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the policy of mutual preferential trade, I think that nothing would be of greater benefit to the farmers of this country if we could obtain
it. The moment that we get a preference in the markets of England every foot of land in this country would increase in value, all the products of the land would increase in value, wages would immediately go up. You could call in all your immigration agents, because all the best immigrants from the British Isles would come to this country. The volume of production would immediately increase, and in a short time the colonies themselves would be able to supply all the food products required in England.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have reminded us that the Minister of Finance did not claim direct credit for the good times. It is true he did not in so many words, but there was running through his speech an assumption that the good times were due, in part at least, to the legislation which this government had enacted. The First Minister, in a speech made, I think, at Bowmanville, touched upon this question in a very ingenious manner. He said that if Providence had blessed the people because the people elected a good government, no one need complain. Well, that was another way of assuming that the good times were due to the government. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that Providence has blessed this country, and it would seem as if Providence, knowing that the hon. gentlemen opposite had made pledges which they could not fulfil, had taken pity on them and had prospered the country so as to enable them to carry out their promises. But although Providence has showered all this wealth upon us, the government still refuse to take the hint, and therefore we are justified in expecting that Providence will punish them for their ingratitude. The Finance Minister in his speech the other day told us that he could see a little cloud arising no bigger than a man's hand. Well, you would suppose that if he was a judicious man, seeing this little cloud arising, he would begin to take in sail and trim for the approaching storm. But he does nothing of the kind ; and I believe that when he next looks up he will see the handwriting on the wall which will seal the doom of his government.

party at that time declared that they would 'sooner fall than stand for the policy that 'we believed to be in the best interests of the country- At that time the county; "which I have the honour to represent was almost purely an agricultural county. when these hon. gentlemen got into power, revenue tariff they would have carried out some one of The Reform the policies they had advocated ? But, not

He was left by 300 majority. This shows conclusively that the great object of the right hon. gentleman was to get into power no matter how, and no matter what policy was to be carried out. In the matter of their preferential tariff the Liberal government has adopted a policy of their own, which will in time hurl them from power. The preference they have given to Great Britain, of 334 per cent, is ruining the second largest industry in Canada, because next to the raising of foodstuffs the clothing of the people is the most Important. The riding I have the honour to represent has five or six woollen mills, and if this policy of the

government is continued it will entail great loss to the people of that constituency. The same remark applies to almost every other constituency in Canada, because most of them have a woollen mill or two within their limits. This policy will reduce the wages of the mechanics and workingmen in these factories, or else it will close them up entirely. I appeal to the government to reconsider their determination not to give more protection to these large manufacturing concerns. The right hon. the Prime Minister has told us that he gives this preference to the English people in order to show our loyalty and good-will towards them, and in the same breath he tells us that the workingmen of England will not pay one cent more for their flour and bread which can be shipped from this country. And so, the right hon. gentleman, just in order to obtain the good-will of England wants to have the wages of Canadian workingmen reduced, and our factories closed. That is the only logical way of looking at his argument. Mr. Speaker, we have been loyal to the British Crown ; we have been loyal to the British Empire ; we sent our soldiers to South Africa to fight the battles of the British Empire. We showed them that the soldiers of Canada are equal to any soldiers on the face of the globe, and these soldiers came out of the factories of Canada which were built up by the national policy. X remember when I was collecting for the Patriotic Fund in my constituency, the workingmen in the woollen mills were the most liberal in subscribing to that fund. I again appeal to this government to reconsider the position they have taken and to treat these workingmen as they deserve to be treated. Now, in reference to the increased quantity of woollen goods which have been imported into this country since the preferential tariff, I find that that increase is close on to #3,000,000, and every cent's worth of these goods should have been manufactured in Canada, and would have been manufactured In Canada had it not been for the preference given to England. In conclusion I call the attention of the government to the following fact. The correspondent of the Galt Reformer, writing on March 12 from Hespeler. a town which is entirely dependent on the woollen industry, makes the following statement:
Another grist of our people are pulling out eastward towards New York state, part of them having gone to-day. The spring exodus bids fair to he a record-breaker.
I shall vote, Mr. Speaker, for the amendment proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition.
